newsitem.title: CHINA: China flood death toll hits 284, typhoons ahead.
newsitem.headline: China flood death toll hits 284, typhoons ahead.

text.p: Floods have wreaked havoc in eastern and southern China with the death toll climbing to 284, officials and international aid workers said on Friday.

Flooding caused by weeks of torrential downpours had killed 25 people and injured 1,067 in the central province of Jiangxi by July 12, Jon Valfells of Iceland, head of media service at the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), quoted Chinese officials as saying.
Chinese officials had earlier put the death toll at 16.
In the eastern province of Zhejiang, the death toll from flooding had doubled to 20 by July 11, Valfells said after visiting the two provinces last month.
Chinese officials and state media have said floods have killed 164 in southwestern Guizhou province, 41 in southern Guangdong province and 34 in neighbouring Guangxi.
The worst could lie ahead. "The Chinese Red Cross is bracing itself for typhoons in Zhejiang," Valfells said in an interview.
Flash floods and swollen river waters slashed Zhejiang's rice output by 380,000 tonnes, with about 344,000 hectares (850,000 acres) of farmland affected, he said.
Torrents measuring up to two metres (6.6 ft) high ravaged Zhejiang, washing away 100 km (62 miles) of dykes, destroying 51,000 houses and damaging 230,000 homes, Valfells said.
Floods have disrupted transportation, telecommunications and electricity, with about 13,800 factories stopping or suspending production, Valfells said.
Video footage showed a towering wave of floodwater sweeping away a 500 metre (1,600 ft) stretch of dykes in Miaoxi village in Zhejiang.
Officials estimated total economic losses in the province at 4.72 billion yuan ($568.7 million).
Jiangxi had been hit more severely than last year, with 271,000 people homeless and direct economic losses estimated at 5.64 billion yuan.
The Chinese Red Cross has sent medical teams to flood-stricken areas to distribute disinfectant and rice.
Flooding is an ancient curse across much of southern China, where summer rains can burst river dykes and inundate towns, cities and huge swathes of farmland.
While floods wreak havoc in the south, drought and high temperatures have been plaguing northern China.
